steps.label: Flowcharts and Pseudocode
steps.content:
Algorithms, Pseudocode and Python

Flowcharts and Pseudocode

Year 8

steps.label: What You Will Learn Today
steps.content:
What You Will Learn Today

Flowcharts and Cambridge Pseudocode both represent the same algorithm, in different forms. Today you learn to convert between them, both ways.

  • Recognise the Terminal, Process, Input/Output and Decision symbols.
  • Turn a flowchart into Cambridge Pseudocode.
  • Turn Cambridge Pseudocode into a flowchart.
  • Explain why DECLARE has no flowchart symbol of its own.

steps.label: Check: Flowchart Symbols
steps.content:
Check: Flowchart Symbols

You met these symbols in Year 7. Match each symbol to its name three times in a row to master it. A wrong answer resets its count back to zero.

steps.label: Refresh: The Four Symbols
steps.content:
Refresh: The Four Symbols

A quick reminder of what each shape means, including one you have not used in a flowchart before: Decision.

steps.label: Every Shape Has a Pseudocode Match
steps.content:
Every Shape Has a Pseudocode Match

Each flowchart shape becomes a specific kind of Cambridge Pseudocode instruction.

  • Terminal (Start/End) - marks where the pseudocode begins and ends. It has no instruction of its own.
  • Process - becomes an assignment line, using the arrow: Name <- Value.
  • Input/Output - becomes INPUT Name when receiving a value, or OUTPUT Name when displaying one.
  • Decision - becomes IF condition THEN, with the Yes path first, then ELSE for the No path, closed with ENDIF.

One shape is missing from this list on purpose

Every NEW variable needs a DECLARE line before it is used. A flowchart has no shape for DECLARE at all - it shows what the algorithm DOES, not each variable's type. You still have to add DECLARE yourself when you write the pseudocode.

steps.label: Check: Match the Shape

items.prompt: Which flowchart shape becomes an assignment line (Name <- Value)?
items.explain: A rectangle (Process) holds an action such as setting a variable.

items.prompt: Which flowchart shape becomes IF ... THEN?
items.explain: A diamond (Decision) always asks a question with two possible paths.

steps.content: Check: Match the Shape

steps.label: Worked Example: Sequence

nodes.text: Ask the user to enter Height

steps.content:
Worked Example: Sequence

Read the flowchart from Start to End, one shape at a time.

Matching Cambridge Pseudocode

DECLARE Height : INTEGER
INPUT Height
OUTPUT Height

DECLARE Height : INTEGER - added even though no shape asked for it, because Height is a brand new variable.
INPUT Height - from the first Input/Output shape.
OUTPUT Height - from the second Input/Output shape.

steps.label: Worked Example: Selection

node.text: Ask the user to enter Mark

steps.content:
Worked Example: Selection

A Decision splits the flowchart into two paths, each ending at its own End.

Matching Cambridge Pseudocode

DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
INPUT Mark
IF Mark >= 50 THEN
  OUTPUT "Pass"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "Fail"
ENDIF

Decision becomes IF ... THEN, Yes first, then ELSE, closed with ENDIF.

steps.label: Activity 1: Flowchart to Pseudocode
steps.content:
Activity 1: Flowchart to Pseudocode

Open Flowchart Blitz and choose Flowchart to Pseudocode from the menu. You will see a flowchart and type the matching Cambridge Pseudocode - remember DECLARE for every new variable.

Before you start

  1. Every flowchart uses sequence, or sequence with one decision - no loops.
  2. One instruction per line.
  3. There is no limit to how many rounds you can practise.

steps.label: Activity 2: Pseudocode to Flowchart
steps.content:
Activity 2: Pseudocode to Flowchart

Open Flowchart Blitz again, this time choose Pseudocode to Flowchart. You will see Cambridge Pseudocode and drag each block into the correct empty shape.

Before you start

  1. DECLARE lines have no shape - skip them.
  2. Drag each remaining block in, in the same order the pseudocode runs.
  3. An IF line's two branches go into the Yes and No slots, not the main line.

Checked Practice: Full Conversion

Now write the whole algorithm yourself.

Task

  • ask for Weight
  • output "Heavy" if Weight is more than 60
  • output "Light" otherwise

Remember

  • DECLARE Weight first.
  • IF ... THEN, ELSE, ENDIF.
